clinicalPearls: Defined by pancytopenia with a hypocellular bone marrow in the absence of abnormal infiltrating cells or fibrosis, reflecting failure of the haematopoietic stem cell compartment
Presentation reflects the affected lineages: fatigue and breathlessness from anaemia, mucocutaneous bleeding and petechiae from thrombocytopenia, and infections from neutropenia
Most cases are acquired and immune-mediated, with T-cell attack on stem cells; drugs, chemicals (e.g. benzene), viral hepatitis (seronegative), and radiation are recognised triggers
Inherited causes such as Fanconi anaemia and dyskeratosis congenita should be considered in younger patients or those with characteristic physical or family features
Severity is graded by degree of neutropenia, reticulocytopenia, and thrombocytopenia; very severe disease carries the highest risk of early death from infection or haemorrhage

Definitive management is either allogeneic stem cell transplant (favoured in younger patients with a matched sibling donor) or immunosuppressive therapy combining antithymocyte globulin and a calcineurin inhibitor
A thrombopoietin receptor agonist can augment haematopoietic recovery when added to immunosuppression
Overlap exists with paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria and hypoplastic myelodysplasia, so flow cytometry for PNH clones and marrow cytogenetics are important at diagnosis
reference.pathophysiology: Aplastic anaemia results from destruction or profound suppression of pluripotent haematopoietic stem cells, leaving an empty (hypocellular) marrow and peripheral pancytopenia. In most acquired cases the mechanism is autoimmune: activated cytotoxic T lymphocytes and their cytokines (interferon-gamma, tumour necrosis factor) drive stem cell apoptosis. Environmental exposures, certain drugs, and viral illness can initiate this immune attack, while inherited marrow failure syndromes reflect defects in DNA repair or telomere maintenance that exhaust the stem cell pool. Clonal disorders such as PNH and MDS can emerge from a damaged marrow because surviving abnormal clones gain a survival advantage.
additionalDifferentials: Marrow infiltration or fibrosis causing pancytopenia
Severe megaloblastic anaemia (B12 or folate deficiency)
Overwhelming infection or hypersplenism causing peripheral cytopenias
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count with reticulocyte count and blood film to confirm pancytopenia and exclude abnormal cells
Bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy to demonstrate hypocellularity and exclude infiltration or dysplasia
Cytogenetic and molecular studies to differentiate from myelodysplasia
Peripheral blood flow cytometry for a PNH clone
Chromosomal fragility testing and telomere length in suspected inherited syndromes
Viral serology (including hepatitis) and screening for autoimmune disease
redFlags: Severe neutropenia with fever, indicating potentially fatal sepsis requiring urgent broad-spectrum antibiotics
Profound thrombocytopenia with mucosal bleeding or signs of intracranial haemorrhage
Rapidly falling counts defining very severe aplastic anaemia and the need for prompt referral to a transplant centre
Emergence of dysplastic or cytogenetic abnormalities suggesting clonal evolution to MDS or leukaemia
reference.prognosis: Untreated severe aplastic anaemia is frequently fatal from infection or bleeding, but outcomes have transformed with early allogeneic transplantation and effective immunosuppression; younger patients with matched sibling donors have high survival, while older patients rely on immunosuppressive therapy with a meaningful risk of relapse and late clonal disease.
pitfalls: Attributing pancytopenia to a peripheral cause and omitting a marrow biopsy that would reveal hypocellularity
Overlooking a coexisting PNH clone or evolving myelodysplasia
Delaying HLA typing and transplant referral in young patients with severe disease
Failing to recognise an inherited marrow failure syndrome, which changes treatment and family counselling
Giving platelet or red cell transfusions without irradiation or leucodepletion in a potential transplant candidate
management: Treat definitively with allogeneic stem cell transplantation, favoured in younger patients with a matched sibling donor
Where transplant is not appropriate, use immunosuppressive therapy combining antithymocyte globulin with a calcineurin inhibitor such as ciclosporin, adding eltrombopag to augment marrow recovery
Provide supportive care with irradiated, leucodepleted red cell and platelet transfusions, minimising exposure to preserve future transplant options
Manage the infection risk from neutropenia with prompt broad-spectrum antibiotics for febrile episodes and antimicrobial prophylaxis
Withdraw implicated drugs and remove toxin exposure such as benzene, and treat seronegative hepatitis-associated disease

Test for a paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria clone and for inherited syndromes (Fanconi anaemia, dyskeratosis congenita) with fragility and telomere studies, guiding treatment and family counselling
Grade severity by blood counts and marrow cellularity to prioritise urgency, and monitor for clonal evolution
